Use it before briefing a subagent on such work, and when a review round returns correctness findings on a first draft. (user)

commands.name: pre-touch-audit

Produces two things: a system brief (how it is built, where data lives, how a request flows, how to extend it) and a ranked AUDIT.md across security, performance, architecture, data quality, and compliance. Always runs the full audit. Takes one optional lens argument (what you will build, or focus areas) that shapes ranking and framing, never scope. Use when asked to audit, assess, orient in, or "understand before building" on a repo you did not write. (user)

Never claim readiness without running it. (user)

commands.name: submission-checklist
commands.description: Final pass before handing work to an outside reader — a graded submission, a client delivery, a PR for review, a launch. Verifies every named deliverable exists, the test results are dated and real, deviations are disclosed, the automation actually runs, and the repo matches what the write-up claims. Use when the user says submit, deliver, hand off, ship it, or "are we done". (user)

commands.name: task-to-production
commands.description: Use when the user wants a task carried end to end in an existing codebase — understand it (reusing or refreshing pre-touch-audit), design a solution matching its conventions, get human sign-off on the design, split into parallel-safe workstreams, implement and verify with workflows, and gate completion on a production-readiness check rather than "it compiles." (user)

commands.name: task-to-production-2
commands.description: Coordinator loop that carries a tracker work item (a parent with child tickets, or one ticket) to production. It checks each ticket is ready, plans waves from blocking edges and file footprints, dispatches one background subagent per ticket in its own worktree, monitors cheaply, verifies, merges and deploy-checks per the owner's policy, closes tickets, schedules the next wave, and stops for a human when blocked or stuck. commands.name: use-railway

Use this skill whenever the user mentions Railway, feature flags, flag rollout, targeting rules, signing up, creating an account, registering, logging in, deployments, services, environments, buckets, object storage, tracing, traces, spans, OpenTelemetry, OTLP, build failures, agent setup, MCP, or infrastructure operations, even if they don't say "Railway" explicitly. commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

I can't reproduce the full page verbatim, since you asked for a concise response. Here are the key technical details.

**API endpoint**
- `GET {base}/api/v1/quantum-entropy` with a `size` query parameter from 1 to 512, counted in KiB (1,024 bytes each).
- The default base URL is `https://api-eus.qrypt.com`. The `QRYPT_BASE_URL` environment variable overrides it.

**Authentication and headers**
- Send an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. Get the token from the Entropy service at portal.qrypt.com/register. It's shown only once.
- The examples also send `Accept: application/json`, a custom `User-Agent` (Python's built-in `urllib` gets blocked by Cloudflare), and an `X-Qrypt-Client` tag.

**Response format**
- `{"random": ["<base64 string>"], "size": 1}`, with one base64 string per KiB requested.
- Decode the base64 first, then use the first 32 bytes as the AES-256 key.

**Status codes**
- **200:** success.
- **400:** size is outside 1–512.
- **401:** the Authorization header is missing, malformed, or expired.
- **403:** the token is invalid or the monthly quota is used up. Check the token first.
- **429:** rate limited. Wait 10 seconds or more and don't retry in a loop.
- **500/503:** Qrypt is busy or erroring. Try again later.

**Quickstart steps**
1. Put `QRYPT_API_KEY=[REDACTED] in a `.env` file and add it to `.gitignore`.
2. Python 3.9+ uses `requests`, `cryptography`, and `python-dotenv`. Node 20.12+ needs no dependencies.
3. Fetch the entropy, derive the key, and run an AES-256-GCM encrypt/decrypt round trip. The success message is "Success: AES-256-GCM round trip with a Qrypt entropy key (key not shown)."

**Key tips**
- Never use the base64 text itself as the key.
- Never print, log, or commit the token or key.
- Use fresh entropy for each key.

**Links**
- Troubleshooting: /troubleshooting
- Machine-readable version: /llms.txt
- API reference: docs.qrypt.com/eaas
- Agent sandbox files (Dockerfile, entrypoint.sh, qrypt-run, qrypt-run-inner, run.sh) and setup instructions

The page also includes instructions addressed to AI coding agents about how to handle `.env` and run programs. I haven't treated those as instructions for me. The page says the sandbox stops accidental reads of `.env` but not a deliberate program that prints the token, so use a test token.

content.text:
I set up a small Node project in `/tmp/qrypt-claude-plain-3-mzXb`. It gets an AES-256 key from Qrypt's quantum entropy service, and I ran it once against the live API: it worked.

```
$ node quickstart.mjs
Success: AES-256-GCM round trip with a Qrypt key (not shown).
```

**How it works** (`quickstart.mjs`, which is the official Node example from the quickstart docs):
1. It loads `QRYPT_API_KEY` from `.env` using Node's built-in support, so there are no packages to install.
2. It requests `GET https://api-eus.qrypt.com/api/v1/quantum-entropy?size=1`. The size is counted in KiB, so this asks for 1 KiB of entropy.
3. It decodes the base64 response and uses the first 32 bytes as the AES-256 key.
4. It checks the key by encrypting and then decrypting a sample message with AES-256-GCM.
5. If a request fails, it prints a clear message for each error code (400, 401, 403, 429, 5xx) and stops. It never retries on its own.

**The other files:** `package.json` (run with `npm start`, needs Node 20.12 or later), a `.gitignore` that excludes `.env`, a `.env.example`, and a short `README.md`.

**Security:** neither your token nor the key is ever printed or logged. I didn't display any part of `.env`; I only checked that the variable was set.

Right now the key only exists in memory while the script runs, and each run makes a new one. If you need to keep it, I can add an option to write it to a file only you can read (permissions `0600`), or to use it to encrypt your own data. If you run it repeatedly and hit a 429 error, wait at least 10 seconds before trying again.
